name: Venture Capital Loss Rates
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Most Bets Lose. That Was Always the Plan.
lesson.summary: Venture capital is built around a power law where most individual investments lose money and a small number of outsized winners carry the fund, which reframes what failure in quantum computing startups actually means for the industry.
lesson.body:
It is a well documented, decades old pattern in venture capital that most individual investments do not return the capital put into them. Widely cited industry data has shown that a large share of VC-backed deals, often estimated near half or more, return less than the original investment, a further share roughly break even or return only a small multiple, and only a small slice, sometimes cited around 5 to 10 percent, deliver the very large returns, 10 times, 50 times, or more, that make a fund's overall economics work. This is called a power law distribution: a few enormous winners generate nearly all of a fund's total profit, while the median individual deal is a loss or a wash.

This reframes how to read news about any single quantum computing startup's struggles or shutdown. A fund does not need every bet to succeed, it needs one or two to succeed spectacularly enough to cover the losses on the rest. A fund can rationally keep investing throughout the VC Funding Frenzy around quantum computing while privately expecting most portfolio companies to end in a mediocre acqui-hire, a quiet shutdown, or a down round, as long as it believes at least one company in the portfolio might become a generational winner. Heavy aggregate VC investment into a sector is therefore not, by itself, proof that professional investors expect the median company in that sector to succeed.

Put a number on it. Suppose a fund invests 10 million dollars each into 10 quantum startups, 100 million total. If 7 return nothing, 2 return their money back at 1 times, and 1 becomes a breakout returning 30 times capital, total returned is 7 times 0 plus 2 times 10 million plus 1 times 300 million, which is 0 plus 20 million plus 300 million, or 320 million dollars against 100 million invested. That is a 3.2 times multiple on invested capital, an excellent overall result, even though 9 of the 10 individual bets were disappointing or outright losses.

This power law dynamic is a crucial corrective against reading any single quantum computing failure as proof the whole sector's investment thesis was wrong, since it was never a per company bet in the way an individual retail investor owning one stock experiences it. But it cuts the other way too: the enormous sums flowing into quantum computing, seen against the stretched multiples in Market Valuation vs Revenue, are not, in aggregate, a signal that most individual companies are expected to become durable, lasting businesses. Most are expected to fail or badly underperform by the fund's own internal portfolio math, priced into the strategy from day one, not treated as a surprise if and when it happens.

Knowing most positions are supposed to lose does not answer the harder question facing anyone already inside a struggling one: when does continued funding stop being patience and start being a mistake.
